title: One corpus divided by name: Plato, Aristotle, Theophrastus and the divided mind
description: Historical theses from Many and One, the authorship notebook and The First Draft holding that the Platonic, Aristotelian and Theophrastan corpora are one body divided by name, and that the divisions are editorial: Andronicus's genuine/spurious partition and his πίνακες, and the single lot of books sold to Apellicon. The page reads ancient legitimacy as standing rather than paternity and sets the esoteric/exoteric partition as an Alexander story told at the seam where corpus meets empire. What Syllogizing Can Divide names the production model as one self-dividing maker, dividing the corpus where De anima III.5 divides mind, and leaves open tests on the ghost catalogues and on epigraphic items not yet held.

claims.statement: This paper names the production model the corpus is consistent with: one self-dividing maker. The ground is III.5's own statement of the structure of mind, a making part and a becoming part related as a craft to its material, and the finding that the corpus divides by name exactly where III.5 divides mind. Heteronymy is that technology (#682): a tool for dividing a mind so that it can make. The masks are what the divided mind looks like from outside. The Platonic, Theophrastan and Aristotelian corpus is what that tool produces, and nothing in it requires another maker.
claims.falsifier: The test of that sentence is the external record, item by item: for each name, what attests a person, where the attestation comes from, and whether it stands outside the manuscript tradition the corpus itself travels in.

claims.registered_title: What Syllogizing Can Divide: De anima III.5, the Divided Mind, and the Socket in God (EA-DIVISION-OF-GOD-01 v0.2)
claims.statement: Fifteen lines, and the largest sustained disagreement in the history of philosophy about a single passage: Alexander making the making mind God from outside; Themistius making it ours; Averroes making it one for all humanity and being condemned for it; Aquinas writing *De unitate intellectus* against him; the faculties legislating on it. Each reader supplied the referent; none could make it hold; the next was required. The passage says the immortal part does not remember. The tradition remembers for it. The perishable mind of III.5 is the commentary tradition, and without it οὐθὲν νοεῖ.
